title: The seven jurists of Medina
hookLine: scholars of the city who kept the Prophet's practice

lines: A BOOK CAN'T SHOW A PAUSE.
cards: Where do you go to learn how the Prophet prayed, once the people who prayed beside him are gone? Books help. But a book can't show you how a hand is raised, or how long a pause is held.
For that, people went to a place. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, had lived in Medina, and Medina remembered.

The children and grandchildren of his Companions grew up on its streets, in the houses where he had eaten and taught. In the Umayyad years, while Damascus held the government, Medina held something else.
Its scholars became well-known as a group: the seven jurists of Medina. Today: the city that kept the practice.

teach.b: These men belonged to the generation Muslims call the Followers, the ones who learned from the Companions. Their names tell the story.

Urwa ibn al-Zubayr was a nephew of Aisha, the Prophet's wife, and passed on a great deal of what she taught. Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad was a grandson of Abu Bakr and, the reports say, grew up in Aisha's care.
Kharija was a son of Zayd ibn Thabit, the Companion who wrote down revelation for the Prophet. And Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, the biographers say, was sought out for his learning on hard questions.
Each stood one step from the Companions themselves.
One wrinkle: the lists agree on most of the names, but differ over the seventh. A well-known group, and its membership is still debated. What did they do?
They answered questions. How do you divide an inheritance? What does a fair sale look like?
They answered from what the Companions had said and done, and from what Medina still did.
When Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz governed the city, the reports say he called its jurists together and promised to act on nothing without their counsel.
A later Medinan scholar, Malik ibn Anas, made this a principle: the practice of the people of Medina. For him, what a whole city had done since the Prophet's day was itself a kind of witness.
Medina became the city of the practice.

how: In the Maliki school of law, the practice of the people of Medina is weighed as evidence alongside the hadith, and students in other schools also learn hadith through chains of teachers that pass through Medina.

games.q: what does “the seven jurists of medina” mean?
o: seven judges appointed by the Umayyad caliph
Medina's scholars, students of the Companions
the seven reciters of the Qur'an's readings

games.q: the seven jurists of Medina — tap the pairs.
p: a son of Zayd ibn Thabit
the practice of the people of Medina

s: every source lists the same seven names
the sources agree on six and name different men as the seventh.
the jurists learned from the Companions of the Prophet
they belonged to the generation called the Followers.
Medina was the seat of the Umayyad government
Damascus held the government; Medina held the memory of the practice.

games.q: you're the new governor of Medina. the city's scholars are well-known, and you hold the power. what do you do?
o: rule on your own and leave the scholars to teach.
call them together and act only with their counsel.
appoint new scholars who agree with you.
games.why: the reports say Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, as governor, gathered Medina's jurists and promised to act on nothing without their counsel.

practice: Here is one report from Aisha: asked what the Prophet did at home, she said he served his family, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray.
Sit with that picture for a few breaths, a man whose words shaped a city helping at home, and bring to mind one small task in your own home that someone else usually does.

wordCard.voice: The seven jurists of Medina. Scholars of the Prophet's city, students of his Companions, who answered questions from what Medina remembered and still did. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the seven jurists, the name later scholars gave Medina's group.

carryVoice: Your line: the city of the practice. Some things a book can't show. Day nine hundred nine, counted.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 676 (Aisha: he served his family, and went out when it was time for prayer)
Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (the Medinan Followers: Urwa, al-Qasim, Kharija, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and others)
al-Tabari, Tarikh (Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz as governor of Medina consulting its jurists)
Malik ibn Anas, al-Muwatta (the practice of the people of Medina)
